title: Next Letter After the Target
statement:
You get a list of lowercase letters letters, sorted in non-decreasing order, and one lowercase letter target. The list contains at least two different letters, and it may repeat letters.

Return the smallest letter in letters that is strictly greater than target. If no letter is greater, the list wraps around: return letters[0].

target does not have to appear in the list.

examples.why: Strictly greater: both copies of "d" are skipped, even though they match the target.
Nothing is greater than "m", so the answer wraps around to the first letter.
The target is smaller than everything, so the first letter is the answer without any wrapping.

constraints: letters is sorted in non-decreasing order
letters has at least two different letters
letters[i] and target are lowercase English letters
hints: The list is sorted. You are looking for the first position whose letter is greater than the target.
That position is an upper bound: everything before it is ≤ target, everything from it on is > target. Binary search finds such a boundary in O(log n).
Search with the condition letters[mid] ≤ target to move right. If the boundary lands at the end of the list, wrap around to index 0.

explain.intuition:
Split the sorted list into two parts: letters that are ≤ target, then letters that are > target. The answer is the first letter of the second part. Because the list is sorted, the split is one clean boundary, and binary search finds a boundary in O(log n) steps.

The wrap-around is just a special boundary: if every letter is ≤ target, the second part is empty and the boundary sits at n. Taking the index modulo n turns that into 0. It is the same idea as a carousel that loops back to the first slide after the last one.
steps: Set lo = 0, hi = n. The boundary lies somewhere in [lo, hi].
While lo < hi, take mid. If letters[mid] ≤ target, the boundary is to the right: lo = mid + 1. Otherwise hi = mid.
When the loop ends, lo is the first index with a letter greater than target, or n if there is none.
pitfalls: Using < instead of ≤ in the comparison. That finds the first letter ≥ target and returns the target itself when it is in the list.
Forgetting the wrap-around and reading letters[n], which is undefined.
Stopping at the first match with the target and returning the next element. With duplicates like ["x", "x", "y"], the next element is another "x".

solutions.title: Linear scan
solutions.idea: Walk the list and return the first letter greater than the target. If the walk ends, return the first letter.

solutions.title: Binary search for the upper bound
solutions.idea: Find the first index whose letter is greater than the target, then wrap with modulo.

followups: The list is a circular buffer that was rotated, so it is sorted starting from some unknown index. Can you still answer in O(log n)?
Return the largest letter strictly smaller than the target instead, wrapping to the last letter. What changes?
lcTitle: Find Smallest Letter Greater Than Target
